title: A connected smooth almost-complement to a central abelian subvariety
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Group schemes and homomorphisms are as in [def-sc-group-scheme], closed and normal subgroups as in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], smoothness as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], connectedness as in [def-weil-connected-scheme], and finite type as in [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Separated means that the diagonal is a closed immersion [def-weil-proper-morphism]. Affine means isomorphic to the spectrum of a commutative ring [def-pc-scheme]. Dimensions are topological Krull dimensions [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. Let $G$ be a smooth connected separated finite-type $k$-group scheme, and let $A\hookrightarrow G$ be a central closed subgroup which is an abelian variety [def-sc-abelian-variety]; central means that its points commute with all points of $G$ after every commutative algebra extension. There is a smooth connected separated finite-type closed normal subgroup $N\hookrightarrow G$ such that multiplication $m:A\times_k N\to G$, $(a,n)\mapsto an$, is a faithfully flat homomorphism of finite presentation with finite scheme-theoretic kernel, and $\dim G=\dim A+\dim N$. Fibre products are [def-pc-fibre-product], finite morphisms are [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], and faithfully flat means flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] and surjective. Finite presentation means locally of finite presentation [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation], quasi-compact and quasi-separated. The product and kernel are scheme-theoretic; no affineness or commutativity assumption is imposed on $G$ or $N$.

source.place: Theorem 8.24 (Rosenlicht decomposition), printed p.153, with connected refinement by taking the identity component of its smooth almost-complement. Proposition 5.23, printed p.104, gives the dimension formula for the product homomorphism with finite kernel; Corollary 1.35 and Summary 1.71 give connected-image surjectivity. No Stacks tag states this decomposition theorem.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-abelian-subgroup-equivariant-multiple-map] to obtain $n>0$ and $\phi:G\to A$. Put $r(g)=\phi(g)-\phi(e)$, a morphism by [def-sc-group-scheme]. Then $r(e)=0$ and $r(i(a))=[n]a$ as morphisms, by substituting $g=e$ in equivariance. To prove homomorphy, consider $h(x,y)=r(xy)-r(x)-r(y):G\times_kG\to A$. It vanishes on both identity axes. The connected $G$ equals its neutral component, so [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component] gives geometric irreducibility. Smoothness gives geometric reducedness by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced]; hence $G$ is geometrically integral. All hypotheses of [lem-sfb-abelian-product-axis-rigidity] hold with $V=W=G$ and both basepoints $e$, so $h=0$. Thus $r$ is a group-scheme homomorphism restricting to $[n]_A$. The differences use commutativity of $A$, supplied by [lem-sc-av-commutative].

source.place: Theorem 8.24, first two sentences, printed p.153; 8.19 expressed by the existing product-axis rigidity statement.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization] to $r:G\to A$: its kernel $K$ is a closed normal finite-type subgroup of $G$. Both groups are separated and finite type, as required (for $A$ this follows from properness in [def-sc-abelian-variety]). Put $N=(K^0)_{\mathrm{red}}$. By [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component], this is a smooth connected integral separated finite-type subgroup with the same space as $K^0$. Its inclusion in $G$ is closed: $K^0\hookrightarrow K$ is clopen, its reduction is closed, and closed immersions compose by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-products].

source.place: Theorem 8.24, kernel construction and last paragraph (perfect-field reduction), with Proposition 1.34 for the connected refinement.

proof.text: The subgroup $N$ is normal scheme-theoretically, not merely on $k$-points. Conjugation gives $c:G\times_kN\to K$ because $r(gng^{-1})=r(g)+0-r(g)=0$. Both $G$ and $N$ are geometrically irreducible by [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component]; hence their product is irreducible by [lem-sc-irreducible-product-over-field]. Its connected image contains $e$, so lies in $K^0$. Factor $c$ through that open subscheme by [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-factors-through-open-subscheme]. The source is reduced: $G$ and $N$ are reduced and tensor products of their affine chart rings are reduced by [lem-weil-pbc-perfect-reduced-tensor], since the algebraically closed $k$ is perfect. The reduced-source factorization in [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-source-factors-through-closed-subscheme] now factors $c$ through $(K^0)_{\mathrm{red}}=N$. Evaluating this morphism on every commutative $k$-algebra gives closure of $N(R)$ under conjugation by $G(R)$, precisely normality in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup].

source.place: Theorem 8.24, normality after perfect-field reduction and taking the neutral component; Stacks Groupoids Tags 0B7R and 047R, expanded via connected image and reduced-source factorization.

proof.text: Let $P=A\times_kN$ with componentwise group law and let $m:P\to G$ be multiplication. For every test algebra, centrality gives $(an)(a^{\prime}n^{\prime})=(aa^{\prime})(nn^{\prime})$, so $m$ preserves multiplication and is a homomorphism by [def-sc-group-scheme]. The scheme $P$ is separated and of finite type: tensor products of finite affine chart algebras are finitely generated, and its diagonal is the product of the closed diagonals of $A$ and $N$, up to rearranging factors; use the product clause of [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-products]. It is nonempty, since it has an identity.

source.place: Theorem 8.24, second paragraph, centrality makes (40) a homomorphism.

proof.text: Let $F=A\times_GN$, the scheme-theoretic intersection. Its projection to $A$ is closed by base change of $N\hookrightarrow G$ in [lem-weil-pbc-proper-fp-permanence](b). As $N\subseteq\ker r$ and $r|_A=[n]$, it factors through $A[n]$. This is a closed immersion: on affine charts a surjection onto the coordinate ring of $F$ factors through the quotient defining $A[n]$ and remains surjective. By [lem-sc-mult-n-isogeny], $A[n]$ is finite. Therefore $F$ is finite by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-finite] and [lem-weil-pbc-finite-composition]. For every test algebra, $an=e$ is equivalent to $n=i(a)^{-1}\in N$. Thus $a\mapsto(a,i(a)^{-1})$ identifies $F$ with $\ker m$; its inverse is first projection. The two composites are identities on points of every test algebra, hence identities of scheme morphisms. In particular the kernel is finite, without any assertion that it is reduced.

source.place: Theorem 8.24, second paragraph: finite intersection and the antidiagonal kernel of (40), with N replaced by its reduced neutral component.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization] to $m:P\to G$. It gives $m=j\circ q$ with $j:I\hookrightarrow G$ a closed subgroup and $q:P\to I$ faithfully flat and of finite presentation. It remains to show that this closed image is all of $G$.

source.place: Theorem 8.24, surjectivity and faithful flatness; Theorem 5.39 replaces the appeal to Summary 1.71.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates], there are finitely many components $K_i$ of $K$, and representatives $k_i\in K(k)$ with $K_i=k_iK^0$. Each $k$-point of $K^0$ belongs to its reduction $N$: a morphism from the reduced $\operatorname{Spec}k$ factors through the reduction by [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-source-factors-through-closed-subscheme]. For any $g\in G(k)$, [lem-sc-isogeny-surjective] gives $a\in A(k)$ with $[n]a=r(g)$, since $n>0$ and $k$ is algebraically closed. Then $i(a)^{-1}g\in K(k)$, so it equals $k_i u$ for some $u\in N(k)$. Centrality of $A$ gives $g=k_i i(a)u\in k_i I(k)$. Thus the finitely many translates $k_i I$ contain all $G(k)$.

source.place: Theorem 8.24, surjectivity from the multiplication map, with the connected refinement justified using Proposition 1.34 and Corollary 1.35.

proof.text: Translation is an isomorphism by [lem-sc-translation-automorphism], so each $k_iI$ is closed in $G$. Their finite union is closed and contains every closed point, since closed points are rational by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base]; it is therefore $|G|$ by [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space]. The scheme $G$ is irreducible by step 1. By the definition of irreducibility, a finite closed covering has a member equal to $|G|$. Translating back gives $|I|=|G|$. Since $G$ is reduced, apply [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-source-factors-through-closed-subscheme] to $\mathrm{id}_G$ and $I\hookrightarrow G$. The resulting section of this closed immersion is its inverse (a closed immersion is a monomorphism), so $j$ is an isomorphism. Consequently $m$ is faithfully flat and of finite presentation.

source.place: Theorem 8.24 with connected refinement: connected-image surjectivity from Corollary 1.35; no equal-dimension matrix-group criterion is used.

proof.text: The finite kernel $F$ has dimension zero: its morphism to $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is surjective since $F$ has the identity, so [lem-sc-finite-surjective-dimension] applies and gives $\dim F=\dim\operatorname{Spec}k=0$. The last equality follows because the spectrum of a field consists of one point.

source.place: Proposition 5.23, printed p.104, preparation for its application to a finite kernel.

proof.text: The factorization theorem [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization] identifies the target $G=I$ of $m$ with the quotient of $P$ by $F=\ker m$. It is also the fpqc coset quotient used in [lem-sfb-homogeneous-quotient-krull-dimension]: $m$ is faithfully flat of finite presentation, hence an fpqc covering, every section of $G$ lifts after pullback along this covering, and two lifts $x,y$ have equal image exactly when $x^{-1}y\in F$. Maps from $P$ constant on cosets descend uniquely by [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent], so $G$ represents the fpqc quotient as well (coverings are [def-weil-pbc-fpqc-covering]); thus the represented quotient schemes agree. The dimension formula gives $\dim P=\dim F+\dim G=\dim G$. Finally [lem-sfb-scheme-product-dimension] gives $\dim P=\dim A+\dim N$. This proves the asserted dimension equality.

source.place: Proposition 5.23, printed p.104, applied to (40), and Theorem 5.39 for the quotient interpretation.

proof_origin.place: Theorem 8.24 and its proof, printed p.153; connected refinement using Proposition 1.34, Corollary 1.35 and reduced components, with Proposition 5.23, p.104 for dimension. Normality and the finite-translate connected refinement are expanded explicitly.
